balcony-waterproofing.q: How much does balcony waterproofing cost in Australia?
balcony-waterproofing.a: Balcony waterproofing costs $30 to $80 per square metre supplied and installed in Australia. A typical 10 square metre balcony runs roughly $300 to $800 depending on membrane type, access and how much of the existing surface needs stripping back before the waterproof membrane and reinforcing bandage go down.

balcony-waterproofing.q: What are the signs a balcony needs waterproofing?
balcony-waterproofing.a: Common warning signs include water stains or mould on the ceiling below the balcony, cracked or bubbling tiles, a spongy or discoloured surface, and water pooling instead of draining to the edge. Any of these point to a failed or ageing membrane and should be checked before internal damage sets in.

balcony-waterproofing.q: Can I waterproof a balcony myself?
balcony-waterproofing.a: Waterproofing a balcony yourself is risky in most of Australia because balcony and wet area waterproofing is licensed work in several states, and DIY jobs commonly fail at flashings, joints and drainage falls. A licensed waterproofer also provides a compliance certificate that insurers and future buyers will want to see.

ceiling-fan-installation.q: How much does it cost to install a ceiling fan in Australia?
ceiling-fan-installation.a: Ceiling fan installation in Australia typically costs $250 to $500 including the fan, based on an electrician's hourly rate of $70 to $130 plus a mid-range ceiling fan with light priced around $270. Costs rise if new wiring, a switch, or ceiling reinforcement is needed for a heavier fan.

ceiling-fan-installation.q: Can I install a ceiling fan myself?
ceiling-fan-installation.a: Wiring a ceiling fan into the mains yourself is illegal in Australia unless you hold an electrical licence, even though the fan itself is simple to mount. A licensed electrician needs to connect it to the switch circuit and confirm the ceiling can support the fan's weight and vibration safely.

ceiling-fan-installation.q: Do I need an electrician to install a ceiling fan?
ceiling-fan-installation.a: Yes, connecting a ceiling fan to household wiring is licensed electrical work in every Australian state, so a qualified electrician must handle the wiring and switch connection even if you buy and hang the fan yourself. This keeps the installation compliant and covered by warranty and insurance.

concrete-repair-and-crack-filling.q: How much does concrete crack repair cost in Australia?
concrete-repair-and-crack-filling.a: Concrete crack repair and patching typically costs $50 to $150 per square metre in Australia, depending on crack severity and surface prep. Small hairline cracks can sometimes be filled for the price of a bag of cement mix, from about $9 to $57, while wider structural cracks need a tradesperson.

Concrete cracks mainly from ground movement, shrinkage as it cures, tree root intrusion, poor drainage saturating the base, or inadequate reinforcing when it was originally poured. Reactive clay soils common across Australia make this worse, which is why cracks often reappear near driveways, paths and slab edges over time.

concrete-repair-and-crack-filling.q: Can I fill a concrete crack myself?
concrete-repair-and-crack-filling.a: Minor hairline cracks can be filled with a cement-based patching compound or crack filler from a hardware store, but wider or spreading cracks usually signal movement in the base and need a tradesperson to assess before repair. Sealing a crack without fixing the underlying cause often means it returns.

engineered-timber-flooring-installation.q: How much does engineered timber flooring cost to install in Australia?
engineered-timber-flooring-installation.a: Engineered timber flooring costs $160 to $250 per square metre installed in Australia, with the timber itself typically around $145 per square metre plus foam underlay at about $14 per square metre and laying labour on top. A 40 square metre living area generally lands between $6,400 and $10,000.

engineered-timber-flooring-installation.q: Is engineered timber flooring better than solid timber?
engineered-timber-flooring-installation.a: Engineered timber flooring is more dimensionally stable than solid timber because its layered plywood core resists expanding and contracting with humidity changes, making it suited to homes with underfloor heating or concrete slabs. Solid timber can be sanded and refinished more times over its life, but engineered boards install faster.

engineered-timber-flooring-installation.q: Can engineered timber flooring be installed over concrete?
engineered-timber-flooring-installation.a: Yes, engineered timber flooring can be glued or floated directly over a concrete slab once the slab is level, dry and tested for moisture. A foam underlay is typically used under a floating installation, and any low spots usually need a self-levelling compound first to stop the boards flexing or creaking.

frameless-shower-screen-installation.q: How much does a frameless shower screen cost in Australia?
frameless-shower-screen-installation.a: A frameless shower screen typically costs $900 to $2,200 supplied and installed in Australia, with the glass panel itself usually priced between $770 and $1,943 depending on size and hardware. Costs increase for larger screens, tinted or textured glass, and fixed panels over a walk-in opening.

frameless-shower-screen-installation.q: What are the disadvantages of a frameless shower screen?
frameless-shower-screen-installation.a: Frameless shower screens use thicker, heavier glass with no frame to catch water, so more water and steam can escape the shower area unless the glass and floor are sealed carefully with silicone. They also cost more upfront than framed or semi-frameless screens and are harder to replace if the glass is damaged.

frameless-shower-screen-installation.q: Do frameless shower screens need a frame at all?
frameless-shower-screen-installation.a: No, frameless shower screens rely on thick 10mm toughened glass, minimal clips and hinges, and a bead of sanitary silicone for support and waterproofing rather than an aluminium frame. This gives a cleaner look but means the glass and hardware need to be fitted precisely by a glazier to stay watertight.

home-rewiring.q: How much does it cost to rewire a house in Australia?
home-rewiring.a: Home rewiring in Australia is charged at an electrician's hourly rate of $70 to $130, since a full rewire is quoted as a project rather than a fixed figure. Cable alone runs about $499 per 100 metre roll, power points around $29 each, and a new switchboard from about $99, on top of labour.

home-rewiring.q: How long does it take to rewire a house?
home-rewiring.a: A full rewire of an average house typically takes an electrician several days to over a week, since every circuit needs to be run through walls and ceilings, tested and connected to a new or upgraded switchboard. Older homes with brick veneer, no roof access or asbestos sheeting can extend the job.

home-rewiring.q: Do I need a new switchboard when rewiring my house?
home-rewiring.a: Most home rewiring jobs include a switchboard upgrade, since old fuse-based boards cannot safely handle the safety switches and circuit breakers required under current wiring rules. A typical 8-way switchboard enclosure costs roughly $87 to $111, and pairing it with new safety switches is standard practice on a full rewire.

kitchen-splashback-installation.q: How much does a kitchen splashback cost to install in Australia?
kitchen-splashback-installation.a: A tiled kitchen splashback typically costs $60 to $180 per square metre supplied and installed, covering tiles priced from $14 to $59 per square metre plus adhesive and grout. A standard 4 to 6 square metre splashback often lands between $250 and $900 depending on the tile chosen.

kitchen-splashback-installation.q: What is the best material for a kitchen splashback?
kitchen-splashback-installation.a: Ceramic and porcelain tiles remain the most popular kitchen splashback material in Australia because they are affordable, heat resistant and easy to clean, with glass and stone splashbacks offering a seamless look at a higher price. The best choice depends on budget, grout preference and how hard the kitchen is used.

kitchen-splashback-installation.q: Can I install a kitchen splashback myself?
kitchen-splashback-installation.a: A ceramic tile splashback is one of the more DIY-friendly tiling jobs since it covers a small, flat, accessible area, but cutting around powerpoints, keeping lines straight and sealing edges properly trip up many first-time tilers. Professional installation adds a modest amount on top of material costs for a cleaner finish.

nbn-point-installation.q: How much does it cost to install an NBN point in Australia?
nbn-point-installation.a: Installing an extra NBN or data point in Australia typically costs $70 to $130 per hour for a licensed electrician or cabler, with a straightforward single point often taking under an hour once cabling is run. Cat6 cable itself costs about $8 to $40 per 305 metre box, so labour is the main cost.

nbn-point-installation.q: Who installs an NBN point, an electrician or NBN Co?
nbn-point-installation.a: NBN Co only installs the connection box at the boundary or wall where the network first enters the home, not extra internal data points. Adding a new NBN or network point elsewhere in the house is done by a licensed electrician or data cabler, separate from the initial NBN Co connection.

nbn-point-installation.q: Can I install an NBN point myself?
nbn-point-installation.a: Running and terminating structured cabling for a new NBN or network point is licensed cabling work in Australia, so it cannot legally be done by an unlicensed homeowner beyond basic patch leads. A licensed technician also tests the finished cable run to confirm it meets Cat6 performance standards before use.

render-crack-repair.q: How much does render crack repair cost in Australia?
render-crack-repair.a: Render crack repair typically costs $30 to $80 per square metre in Australia, depending on crack width and how much surrounding render needs cutting back. Small hairline cracks can sometimes be patched with a flexible gap filler from around $6 to $23 a cartridge, while wider cracks need a render mix and a tradesperson.

Render cracks mainly from building movement, shrinkage as the render cures, moisture getting behind the surface, or render applied too thick over a poorly prepared wall. Hairline cracking is common and often cosmetic, but wider or spreading cracks can let water into the wall and should be checked promptly.

render-crack-repair.q: Can I repair render cracks myself?
render-crack-repair.a: Small hairline cracks can be filled with a flexible exterior gap filler as a temporary fix, but matching the texture and colour of existing render is difficult without the right tools and mix ratio. For a durable, near-invisible repair, especially on wider cracks, a rendering tradesperson gets a better long-term result.

security-camera-and-cctv-wiring.q: How much does it cost to install CCTV cameras in Australia?
security-camera-and-cctv-wiring.a: CCTV installation in Australia typically costs $70 to $130 per hour for a licensed electrician, with a 4-camera kit priced from about $89 to $399 depending on resolution and features. A standard home system with wiring and setup often totals a few hundred to over a thousand dollars depending on camera count.

security-camera-and-cctv-wiring.q: Do I need an electrician to install security cameras?
security-camera-and-cctv-wiring.a: Wireless battery or Wi-Fi cameras can usually be mounted without an electrician, but wired CCTV systems that run cable back to a recorder or need extra power points should be installed by a licensed electrician or data cabler. This keeps the wiring compliant and avoids exposed cable runs around the house.

security-camera-and-cctv-wiring.q: Where should security cameras be placed on a house?
security-camera-and-cctv-wiring.a: Cameras are generally placed covering the front door, driveway, back entry and any side access points hidden from the street, mounted high enough to avoid tampering but low enough to capture faces clearly. Avoid pointing cameras directly into strong backlight like a rising or setting sun, which washes out footage.

stone-benchtop-installation.q: How much does a stone benchtop cost in Australia?
stone-benchtop-installation.a: A stone benchtop typically costs $800 to $1,320 per square metre supplied in Australia, plus fabrication and fitting by a stonemason. An average kitchen benchtop of around 5 square metres often lands between $4,800 and $7,500 installed, once edge profiling and cutouts for sinks and cooktops are added.

stone-benchtop-installation.q: Is engineered stone still allowed in Australia?
stone-benchtop-installation.a: No, working with engineered stone benchtops was banned nationally from 1 July 2024 due to the silicosis risk from cutting and polishing the material. Tradespeople can no longer fabricate or install new engineered stone benchtops, so homeowners now choose porcelain, natural stone or laminate for new kitchens instead.

stone-benchtop-installation.q: What can I use instead of engineered stone for a benchtop?
stone-benchtop-installation.a: Since engineered stone was banned in Australia from 1 July 2024, popular alternatives include porcelain benchtops, which resist heat and scratches well, and natural stone like granite or marble, both priced in a similar range to what engineered stone previously cost. Laminate remains the budget option for tighter renovations.

vinyl-plank-installation.q: How much does vinyl plank flooring cost to install in Australia?
vinyl-plank-installation.a: Vinyl plank flooring costs $40 to $150 per square metre installed in Australia, with the planks themselves typically priced between $25 and $64 per square metre depending on thickness and finish. A 30 square metre living area generally costs $1,200 to $4,500 fitted, with extra for levelling an uneven subfloor.

Most rigid vinyl plank flooring sold in Australia is fully waterproof at the board level, built with a solid core rather than the fibreboard core used in laminate, so it handles spills and damp areas like kitchens and laundries well. The seams and edges still need correct installation to stop water tracking underneath.

vinyl-plank-installation.q: Does vinyl plank flooring need underlay?
vinyl-plank-installation.a: Vinyl plank flooring often includes an attached foam or cork backing, but a separate underlay is still recommended over concrete or uneven timber subfloors for extra sound dampening and comfort underfoot. Any dips or high spots in the subfloor usually need a self-levelling compound before the planks go down.
